title: Cloud Computing: Compute, Storage, Networks and IAM
sub: Choose between VMs, containers and functions, plan a VPC, lock down access with IAM, describe it all as code and keep the bill under control
goals: Explain IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and functions, and where the shared-responsibility line falls for each
Containerise a service and run it locally with the right port and bind address
Plan VPC address space and predict reachability from routes, public IPs and security groups
Read and write IAM policies, and explain how explicit deny, allow and default deny combine
Describe infrastructure as code with Terraform or OpenTofu, and keep a learning account safe and cheap

blocks.text: "The cloud" is other people's computers, rented by the minute through an API. That sentence is glib but useful: everything in     the last three chapters still applies. Cloud servers are Linux machines running services behind reverse proxies, managed through     REST APIs, protected with TLS and signed requests. What changes is that the network, the disks, the firewalls and even the     permissions are now software you configure, mostly with JSON, and mistakes are one API call away from the whole internet. This chapter     uses AWS names because they are the most common, and gives the Azure and Google Cloud equivalents. You do not need an account to do     the labs: the VPC and IAM simulators, the Python and the container work all run on your Mac or in this page.
What you are actually renting

NIST's definition (SP 800-145) names five characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling,     rapid elasticity and measured service. In plain words: you get resources through an API in seconds, from anywhere, sharing hardware     with other customers, scaling up and down, and paying for what you use. Services come in layers, and the higher you go the less you     manage and the less you control:

You manage

blocks.title: Service models

blocks.code:
⟪w:SHARED RESPONSIBILITY⟫ (IaaS shown; it shifts left as you move up to PaaS and SaaS)

⟪y:YOU⟫  data  ·  who can access it (IAM)  ·  application  ·  OS patches  ·  firewall rules  ·  encryption settings
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
⟪c:PROVIDER⟫  physical security  ·  hardware  ·  hypervisor  ·  the network between data centres  ·  the API itself

blocks.text: Most cloud breaches happen on the *you* side of that line: a storage bucket left public, a key committed to GitHub, a security     group open to the world, an unpatched VM. The provider's side rarely fails. That is why this chapter spends as long on networks and     permissions as on servers.
Regions, zones and latency

A **region** is a geographic area such as `us-east-1` (northern Virginia) or `eu-west-2` (London). Each region has several     **availability zones** (AZs): separate data centres with their own power and cooling, a few milliseconds apart. Spread a service across     two or more AZs and one building can fail without taking you down. Pick a region by where your users are, which laws apply to the data,     which services exist there and the price, which differs between regions.

blocks.out:
London to Dublin            460 km   round trip at least   4.6 ms
London to Frankfurt         640 km   round trip at least   6.4 ms
London to N. Virginia      5900 km   round trip at least  59.0 ms
London to Sydney          17000 km   round trip at least 170.0 ms
A page that needs 10 sequential requests to Sydney waits at least 1700 ms

blocks.text: No amount of money removes that floor. It is why CDNs cache content near users, why chatty APIs feel slow across oceans, and why     the database should sit in the same region (ideally the same AZ) as the code that queries it.
Compute: VMs, containers and functions

A **virtual machine** (EC2 instance, Azure VM, Compute Engine instance) is the closest thing to your own server: you pick an image     (Ubuntu, Debian, Amazon Linux), a size (CPUs and memory), a disk and a network, and you get SSH access. Everything from the Server Basics     chapter applies unchanged. A **container** packages an application with its dependencies so it runs the same on your Mac and in the cloud.     A **function** is a single handler that the platform runs on demand.
Containers

A container image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata (which command to run, which port it listens on). A     container is a running process from that image, isolated with Linux namespaces and limited with cgroups. It is not a VM: it shares the     host's kernel, starts in milliseconds and adds almost no overhead. On a Mac, containers run inside a small Linux VM that Docker Desktop,     OrbStack or colima manages for you. Here is a `Dockerfile` for the API from Server Basics:

blocks.code:
# Small official Python base image
FROM python:3.13-slim

# Don't run as root inside the container
RUN useradd --create-home app
WORKDIR /app
COPY api_server.py .
USER app

# The server must listen on all interfaces inside the container,
# so change its bind address from 127.0.0.1 to 0.0.0.0 (or read it from an env var).
ENV HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=8080
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health', timeout=2)" || exit 1
CMD ["python", "api_server.py"]

docker build -t labapi:1.0 .
docker run -d --name labapi -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 labapi:1.0
docker ps
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
docker logs -f labapi
docker stop labapi && docker rm labapi

tokens.exp: detached: run in the background and print the container ID
a name to use instead of the ID in later commands
host address : host port : container port. Without the address, Docker publishes on every interface
image name and tag: never deploy `latest`, you cannot tell what it was

blocks.title: Inside a container, 127.0.0.1 is the container

blocks.text: `api_server.py` binds to `127.0.0.1`, which inside the container means "only programs in this container". Docker forwards     published ports to the container's network interface, so the server must bind to `0.0.0.0`. Change the two lines in `__main__` to read     `os.environ.get("HOST", "127.0.0.1")` and `int(os.environ.get("PORT", 8080))`. This is the most common "works locally, not in Docker"     problem.

blocks.name: docker
blocks.sum: Build container images and run, inspect, log and stop containers.
blocks.syntax: docker build -t NAME:TAG DIR        docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [CMD]        docker ps | logs | exec | stop | rm

how.text: `docker` is a client for a daemon that builds images and runs containers. `build` reads a `Dockerfile` and produces an image, caching each instruction as a layer so unchanged steps are instant next time (order instructions from least to most frequently changing). `run` creates a container from an image; `exec` runs another command inside a running one.

Images are referenced as `registry/name:tag`. Cloud platforms pull images from a registry such as Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR or Google Artifact Registry, so deploying usually means `docker push` followed by telling the platform the new tag.
On macOS, Docker Desktop, OrbStack and colima all provide the `docker` command and a Linux VM to run it in. Check the licence terms of Docker Desktop for work use.

gotchas: Secrets passed with `-e` or written in a `Dockerfile` end up in `docker inspect` output or in image layers. Use your platform's secret store.
On Linux hosts, published ports bypass `ufw` rules (see Server Basics). Publish to `127.0.0.1` when a reverse proxy sits in front.

blocks.text: Functions

With **FaaS** you upload a handler, and the platform runs it when an event arrives: an HTTP request, a file landing in storage,     a message on a queue, a timer. You pay per invocation and per millisecond, and nothing runs (or costs) when there are no events. The     catch is the **cold start**: the first call after a quiet period waits while the platform starts a fresh environment. An AWS Lambda     handler in Python is just a function, so you can call it locally with a sample event exactly as the platform would:

Same idea as the WSGI app in Server Basics: keep the logic in a plain function, and the platform becomes a detail you can test     without. Functions suit spiky or occasional work (webhooks, thumbnails, scheduled jobs). Long-running, steady or latency-critical     services are usually cheaper and simpler as containers or VMs.

blocks.text: **Object storage** is the cloud's most important invention. A **bucket** holds objects addressed by a **key** such as     `reports/2026/q3.csv`: the slashes are just characters, not real folders. You read and write whole objects through a REST API (`PUT`     and `GET`), it scales to any size, and S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability by storing copies across several AZs.     Objects are private by default; since April 2023, new S3 buckets block public access unless you deliberately turn that off.

To give someone temporary access to one private object without making it public or sharing your keys, generate a **presigned     URL**: a link whose query string carries an expiry time and an HMAC signature made with your credentials (the same idea as the webhook     signatures in the APIs chapter). Anyone with the link can download that object until it expires, and nothing else.

blocks.code:
aws s3 mb s3://lab-reports-$RANDOM
aws s3 cp report.csv s3://lab-reports-12345/2026/q3.csv
aws s3 ls s3://lab-reports-12345 --recursive --human-readable
aws s3 presign s3://lab-reports-12345/2026/q3.csv --expires-in 3600
aws s3 sync ./site s3://lab-reports-12345/site --delete

blocks.name: aws
blocks.sum: The AWS command-line interface: every AWS API, as subcommands, from your terminal.
blocks.syntax: aws SERVICE COMMAND [--options] [--profile NAME] [--region REGION] [--output json|table|text]

how.text: `aws` turns each AWS API call into a command: `aws ec2 describe-instances` is the `DescribeInstances` API. It signs every request with your credentials using SigV4 (an HMAC-based scheme), sends it over HTTPS, and prints the JSON response. `--query` filters the output with JMESPath, so you rarely need `jq`.

Credentials come from `aws configure sso` (single sign-on, preferred), environment variables, or `~/.aws/credentials`. `--profile` picks a named set. Long-lived access keys on a laptop are the classic way accounts get compromised: prefer SSO with short-lived credentials.
Azure has `az` and Google Cloud has `gcloud`; they follow the same pattern of service, verb and JSON output.

flags.d: JMESPath filter on the JSON output
print which account and identity you are using: run it first, every time

gotchas: Commands act on whatever account and region your profile points at. A habit of `aws sts get-caller-identity` before anything destructive prevents the worst mistakes.

blocks.text: Networking: VPCs, subnets and security groups

A **VPC** (virtual private cloud; a VNet in Azure) is your own private network in a region, with an address range you choose from     the private blocks you met in the addressing chapter. You divide it into **subnets**, each in one availability zone. What makes a subnet     "public" or "private" is not a setting on the subnet but its **route table**:

head: Piece
What it does
Lives where
rows: decides where packets for each destination go; every table has a `local` route for the VPC range
connects the VPC to the internet and translates public IPs
its route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to the IGW
lets instances without public IPs start outbound connections (updates, APIs), but accepts none inbound
its route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to a NAT gateway, or nowhere
a **stateful** firewall on each instance: allow rules only, deny by default, replies allowed automatically
a **stateless** filter on each subnet: allow and deny rules, both directions checked
blocks.title: The parts of a VPC

blocks.text: Planning the address space is the `ipaddress` work from the addressing chapter. Leave room to grow: you cannot shrink a VPC later,     and overlapping ranges make it impossible to connect two VPCs or your home network over a VPN:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress

vpc = ipaddress.ip_network("10.20.0.0/16")
subnets = list(vpc.subnets(new_prefix=20))         # 16 blocks of 4096 addresses
plan = {
    "public-a": subnets[0], "public-b": subnets[1],
    "private-a": subnets[4], "private-b": subnets[5],
    "data-a": subnets[8], "data-b": subnets[9],
}
for name, net in plan.items():
    usable = net.num_addresses - 5                  # AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet
    print(f"{name:<10} {str(net):<15} {usable:>5} usable")
print("spare /20 blocks for later:", len(subnets) - len(plan))
print("overlaps home LAN 192.168.1.0/24?", vpc.overlaps(ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/24")))
blocks.out:
public-a   10.20.0.0/20     4091 usable
public-b   10.20.16.0/20    4091 usable
private-a  10.20.64.0/20    4091 usable
private-b  10.20.80.0/20    4091 usable
data-a     10.20.128.0/20   4091 usable
data-b     10.20.144.0/20   4091 usable
spare /20 blocks for later: 10
overlaps home LAN 192.168.1.0/24? False

blocks.text: Now wire it up. The lab below is a small VPC: a web server and a NAT gateway in a public subnet, a database in a private one. The     seven tests show who can reach what, and each one expands to the reasoning a cloud network actually applies. Break it on purpose: remove     routes, add public IPs, open ports to the world, and read which step fails.

Why does giving `db` a public IP not make it reachable? Why does removing the public route break `db`'s updates even though `db` is in     the *private* subnet? Which single rule in `db-sg` is better than "Postgres from the whole VPC", and why? Why does a blocked connection look     like a timeout to the client, not a refusal?
IAM: who may do what

Every cloud API call is checked against **IAM** (identity and access management). A **principal** (a user, a role assumed by a     service or a person, or another account) makes a **request** (an action such as `s3:GetObject` on a **resource** such as     `arn:aws:s3:::lab-reports/2026/q3.csv`), and **policies** decide. Policies are JSON documents of statements:

The evaluation logic, simplified to one account, has three rules. Everything starts **denied**. A matching `Allow` statement     allows. A matching `Deny` statement overrides any number of allows. `Version` is the policy language version, always `2012-10-17`, not     a date you change. Test that in the simulator below, then try the "Far too broad" preset with `iam:CreateAccessKey`: `"Action": "*"` on     `"Resource": "*"` is a full administrator, and is the policy most often found attached to leaked keys.

items.text: **Least privilege**: grant the specific actions on the specific resources a job needs, and nothing else. Start narrow and add; it is much harder to take permissions away later.
**Roles, not keys**: give a VM, container or function a *role*, and the platform hands it short-lived credentials that rotate automatically. Nothing to leak in code.
**Humans through single sign-on with MFA**, never through long-lived access keys in `~/.aws/credentials`.
**Guardrails at the top**: organisations can attach policies (AWS SCPs, Azure Policy) that no one below can override, for example "never disable logging" or "only these regions".

blocks.title: A tiny policy evaluator

task.text: Write `decide(policy, action, resource)` that returns `"allow"`, `"explicit-deny"` or `"implicit-deny"` for a policy shaped like the        JSON above, without conditions. `Action` and `Resource` may be a string or a list. Wildcards: `*` matches any run of characters, and        actions compare case-insensitively (resources do not). Use `fnmatch.fnmatchcase` and lower-case the action and pattern yourself.

hints: Collect every statement that matches first, then decide: any Deny wins, then any Allow, otherwise the default.
`fnmatchcase("s3:getobject", "s3:get*")` is True; `fnmatch` without `case` would follow the operating system's case rules, which differ between macOS and Linux.

why.text: Evaluating all matching statements before deciding is the point: the order of statements in a policy never matters, and one        Deny anywhere beats every Allow. Real IAM adds conditions, `NotAction`, resource policies, permission boundaries and organisation        policies, but each of those is another place a Deny can come from or an Allow must also exist.

blocks.check:
P = {"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:Get*", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::lab/*"},
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::lab/*"},
    {"Effect": "Deny", "Action": "s3:DeleteObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::lab/keep/*"}]}
assert decide(P, "s3:GetObject", "arn:aws:s3:::lab/a.txt") == "allow", "Get* should allow GetObject"
assert decide(P, "S3:GETOBJECT", "arn:aws:s3:::lab/a.txt") == "allow", "Actions compare case-insensitively"
assert decide(P, "s3:GetObject", "arn:aws:s3:::LAB/a.txt") == "implicit-deny", "Resources compare case-sensitively"
assert decide(P, "s3:DeleteObject", "arn:aws:s3:::lab/a.txt") == "allow", "DeleteObject on lab/a.txt is allowed"
assert decide(P, "s3:DeleteObject", "arn:aws:s3:::lab/keep/x") == "explicit-deny", "The Deny must override the Allow"
assert decide(P, "s3:ListBucket", "arn:aws:s3:::lab") == "implicit-deny", "Nothing allows ListBucket"
one = {"Statement": {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*"}}
assert decide(one, "iam:CreateUser", "anything") == "allow", "Statement may be a single object, and * matches everything"

blocks.text: Infrastructure as code

Clicking through a web console is fine for learning and terrible for anything you need twice. **Infrastructure as code** describes     resources in files that live in Git: you review changes like code, recreate an environment from scratch, and see exactly what will change     before it changes. Terraform and its open-source fork OpenTofu use the same HCL language and work with every major cloud. This file creates     a private, versioned S3 bucket:

blocks.code:
brew install hashicorp/tap/terraform
terraform init
terraform fmt && terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply
terraform destroy

blocks.text: `plan` is the important one: it compares the files with what exists and prints every create, change and destroy before anything     happens. Read it every time, especially lines that say `must be replaced`. Terraform records what it manages in a **state** file; for     anything shared, keep state in remote storage with locking, never in Git, because it can contain secrets. OpenTofu installs with     `brew install opentofu` and uses `tofu` in place of `terraform`.
Cost and safety

Cloud bills are usage-based, which is wonderful until something runs that you forgot about. New AWS accounts now start on a     credit-based free plan with spending limits, and Azure and Google Cloud offer trial credits plus always-free tiers; the details change     often, so read each provider's current terms before you create resources. Whatever the provider, these habits keep a learning account     cheap:

items.text: **Set a budget alarm on day one** (AWS Budgets, Azure Cost Management, Google Cloud Billing budgets) at a figure you would not mind losing.
**Turn on MFA for the root account**, then stop using it. Work as an SSO user or IAM user with limited permissions.
**Tag everything** with `project` and `owner`, so you can find and delete it later.
**Destroy what you are not using**: `terraform destroy`, or delete the stack. Stopped VMs still pay for their disks and public IPv4 addresses.
**Watch the quiet costs**: NAT gateways bill by the hour and per gigabyte, data leaving the cloud (egress) costs money, and public IPv4 addresses are charged by the hour on AWS.

blocks.code:
# Example rates for illustration only: real prices differ by provider, region and date.
RATES = {
    "small VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB)": (0.04, "hour"),
    "public IPv4 address": (0.005, "hour"),
    "NAT gateway": (0.045, "hour"),
    "NAT data processed": (0.045, "GB"),
    "object storage": (0.023, "GB-month"),
    "data out to the internet": (0.09, "GB"),
}
usage = {"small VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB)": 730, "public IPv4 address": 730, "NAT gateway": 730,
         "NAT data processed": 50, "object storage": 200, "data out to the internet": 100}

total = 0
for item, qty in usage.items():
    rate, unit = RATES[item]
    cost = rate * qty
    total += cost
    print(f"{item:<26} {qty:>5} {unit:<9} ${cost:7.2f}")
print(f"{'monthly total':<42} ${total:7.2f}")
print(f"the NAT gateway alone is {100 * (RATES['NAT gateway'][0] * 730 + 0.045 * 50) / total:.0f}% of the bill")
blocks.out:
small VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB)      730 hour      $  29.20
public IPv4 address          730 hour      $   3.65
NAT gateway                  730 hour      $  32.85
NAT data processed            50 GB        $   2.25
object storage               200 GB-month  $   4.60
data out to the internet     100 GB        $   9.00
monthly total                              $  81.55
the NAT gateway alone is 43% of the bill

blocks.text: The surprise in that estimate is typical: the NAT gateway costs more than the server it serves. In a learning account, a private     subnet that needs only occasional updates can use VPC endpoints for the provider's own services, or simply be short-lived.
Cloud, homelab or both?

head: Question
Homelab

rows: per hour and per GB; can surprise you

blocks.text: You do not have to choose. A common path is to learn Linux, services and networking on a Raspberry Pi or a homelab VM, where     mistakes cost nothing, then reproduce the same service in the cloud with Terraform. Tools such as Tailscale or Cloudflare Tunnel connect     the two without opening ports on your router.

blocks.title: Design a small deployment

task.text: You are deploying the lab API with a PostgreSQL database for a small team. Describe: which subnets the API, the database and a load        balancer go in; the inbound rules of each security group; how the API gets the database password; how you would deploy a new version;        and two things you would set up on day one to avoid a surprise bill or breach.

hints: Follow a request from the internet inward and allow only the previous hop at each layer.
Every secret needs a home that is not code, an image or Git.
blocks.solution:
Load balancer in public subnets in two AZs; security group allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0.
API containers (or VMs) in private subnets in two AZs; security group allows 8080 only from the load balancer's security group.
Database (managed, e.g. RDS) in private data subnets; security group allows 5432 only from the API's security group. No public IPs anywhere except the load balancer.
Database password in a secret store (Secrets Manager / Key Vault / Secret Manager), read at start-up by the API through its IAM role; nothing in the image or the repository.
Deploy by building and pushing a new image tag, then updating the service (rolling update behind the health check), all described in Terraform and applied after reading terraform plan.
Day one: a budget alarm, MFA on the root account with SSO for people, CloudTrail (audit logging) on, and tags on every resource.

why.text: The pattern, public entry point, private application, more private data, each layer accepting traffic only from the layer in        front of it, is the same whether you use VMs, containers or functions. Referring to security groups instead of IP ranges keeps the rules        correct as instances come and go.

questions.q: In IaaS, who patches the operating system of your VM?

options.text: Nobody; cloud VMs do not need patches

questions.why: IaaS gives you a machine. Everything from the OS up, including patches and firewall rules, is on your side of the shared-responsibility line.

options.text: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway
It uses public IP addresses for its range
It has a NAT gateway in it

questions.why: Routing decides. An instance in that subnet also needs a public IP and a security group that allows the traffic.

questions.q: A security group allows inbound 443. Do you also need an outbound rule for the replies?

options.text: No: security groups are stateful and allow replies to allowed traffic

questions.why: Stateful filters track connections. Network ACLs are stateless and do need rules for both directions.

questions.q: A policy allows `s3:*` on a bucket, and another attached policy denies `s3:DeleteObject`. Can the user delete objects?

options.text: Yes, because s3:* is more general
No: an explicit Deny overrides any Allow

questions.why: Order never matters in IAM. One matching Deny wins.

questions.q: Why should a container's server bind to 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1?

options.text: Published ports arrive on the container's network interface, not its loopback

questions.why: Inside the container, loopback is the container itself. Port publishing forwards to the container's own interface.

questions.q: Which command should you read carefully before every infrastructure change?
questions.why: `plan` shows every create, change and destroy before it happens. Lines saying a resource must be replaced deserve extra attention.

blocks.title: Ship the lab API: container, scan, deploy

blocks.text: Take the API from Server Basics all the way to something deployable, with every step reproducible from files in one Git             repository. Parts 1 to 3 need only your Mac. Part 4 is optional and uses a cloud account with a budget alarm set first.
1. Containerise

Make the bind address and port come from environment variables, build the image from this chapter's `Dockerfile`, run it with             the port published to `127.0.0.1`, and confirm `docker ps` shows the container as `healthy` after the health check has run.
2. Make it twelve-factor friendly

Log to stdout only (the platform collects it), read every setting from the environment, and handle `SIGTERM` by finishing the             current request and exiting, which is how platforms stop containers during a deploy. Test with `docker stop`, which sends `SIGTERM`             and waits ten seconds before killing.
3. Check what you ship

List the image's size and layers with `docker history labapi:1.0`. Scan it for known vulnerabilities with a scanner such as             Trivy (`brew install trivy`, then `trivy image labapi:1.0`) and note which findings come from the base image. Try a smaller base and             compare.
4. Deploy (optional, with a budget alarm in place)

items.text: Push the image to a registry (GitHub Container Registry is free for public images).
Run it on a managed container platform (Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, or AWS App Runner or ECS on Fargate), described in Terraform or OpenTofu.
Give it a role with no permissions at all, since it needs none, and confirm with the provider's IAM tools.
Point `watch_api.zsh` from Server Basics at the public URL, then `terraform destroy` and check the bill the next day.

blocks.text: 5. Stretch goals

items.text: Add a managed database in a private subnet and store its password in the platform's secret store.
Put the service behind a custom domain with an automatically renewed certificate, and check it with `openssl s_client`.

terms.def: infrastructure, platform and software as a service: how much of the stack the provider runs for you
a geographic area containing several availability zones
one or more data centres in a region with independent power and networking
an isolated process started from an image of filesystem layers, sharing the host kernel
the extra delay when a serverless platform must start a fresh environment for a function
a service that stores whole files as objects addressed by key in buckets, over an HTTP API
a time-limited link to one private object, authorised by a signature in its query string
virtual private cloud: a private network in a region, divided into subnets
a stateful, allow-only firewall attached to cloud instances
lets private instances make outbound connections without accepting inbound ones
identity and access management: principals, policies and the rules that evaluate requests
granting only the permissions a task needs, on only the resources it needs
describing cloud resources in versioned files that a tool such as Terraform applies
